units.excerpt: It does not mean we would redact information merely because it is sensitive or to reduce the risk of a leak.
units.paraphrase: Sensitivity alone or leak-risk reduction does not justify redaction.

units.excerpt: The external review will address:
units.paraphrase: The following topics will be covered by the external review.

units.excerpt: Adequacy of information: Whether the Risk Report contains sufficient information to assess the identified risks;
units.paraphrase: The review assesses whether the Risk Report has enough information to evaluate identified risks.

units.excerpt: Analytical rigor: The strength of the Risk Report’s reasoning and analysis;
units.paraphrase: The review evaluates the strength of the report's reasoning and analysis.

units.excerpt: Areas of disagreement: Whether the external reviewer disagrees with any of the Risk Report’s key claims and, if so, the reasons for any such disagreements; and
units.paraphrase: The review notes any disagreements with the report's key claims and the reasons for them.

units.excerpt: Risk reduction recommendations: Recommendations for further reducing identified risks.
units.paraphrase: The review provides recommendations for further reducing identified risks.

units.excerpt: The external reviewer will also evaluate our redaction decisions while avoiding disclosure of the redacted content itself.
units.paraphrase: The reviewer evaluates redaction decisions without disclosing the redacted content.

units.excerpt: In particular, the review will cover:
units.paraphrase: The review covers specific redaction-related topics.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Redaction scope: The general nature and scope of redactions;
units.paraphrase: The review addresses the general nature and scope of redactions.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Redaction justification: Whether the external reviewer generally agrees or disagrees with the publicly stated reasons for the redactions and, if relevant, the reasons for any disagreements;
units.paraphrase: The review addresses reviewer agreement or disagreement with stated redaction justifications.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Balancing test: Whether the redactions strike a reasonable balance between Anthropic’s legitimate interests and society’s interest in transparency; and
units.paraphrase: The review assesses whether redactions balance Anthropic's interests against societal transparency interests.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Materiality: Whether any of the redactions in the public report are material to any of the external reviewer’s substantive disagreements with the report’s claims.
units.paraphrase: The review assesses whether redactions are material to the reviewer's substantive disagreements with the report.

units.excerpt: We will ask the external reviewer to memorialize its findings on the topics above in a written report that is made public.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers are asked to document findings in a written report that is published.

units.excerpt: External reviewers will be bound by obligations not to disclose confidential information (e.g., confidential intellectual property, matters of national security, or proprietary details such as model architecture, cost, or size), but beyond that will not be restricted in what they can publish, including concerns about the Risk Report or Anthropic’s conduct in connection with the external review.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers must keep specified confidential information private but otherwise face no restriction on publishing, including criticisms of the report or Anthropic's conduct.

units.excerpt: We commit to the following governance measures to promote internal and external accountability.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic states it commits to governance measures for internal and external accountability.

units.excerpt: Responsible Scaling Officer: We will maintain the position of RSO, a designated member of staff who is responsible for the implementation of this policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain a Responsible Scaling Officer role responsible for policy implementation.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: as needed, proposing updates to this policy
units.paraphrase: One RSO duty is proposing policy updates as needed.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: approving relevant model development or deployment decisions based on our risk assessments
units.paraphrase: Another RSO duty is approving model development or deployment decisions based on risk assessments.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: reviewing major contracts (e.g., deployment partnerships) for consistency with this policy
units.paraphrase: Another RSO duty is reviewing major contracts for consistency with the policy.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: overseeing the implementation of this policy, including the allocation of sufficient resources
units.paraphrase: Another RSO duty is overseeing policy implementation including resource allocation.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: receiving and addressing reports of potential instances of noncompliance
units.paraphrase: Another RSO duty is receiving and addressing noncompliance reports.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: making judgment calls on policy interpretation and application
units.paraphrase: Another RSO duty is making judgment calls on interpreting and applying the policy.

units.excerpt: Long Term Benefit Trust: We will regularly brief the LTBT on plans and developments related to our Risk Reports, including model training, capability evals, mitigations, and risk analyses.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will regularly brief the LTBT on Risk Report-related plans and developments.

units.excerpt: Internal transparency: We will share final, unredacted Risk Reports with Anthropic's regular-clearance staff.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will share final unredacted Risk Reports with regular-clearance staff.

units.excerpt: Noncompliance reporting: We will maintain a process for Anthropic staff to submit anonymous or identified reports regarding potential noncompliance with this policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain a process for staff to submit anonymous or identified noncompliance reports.

units.excerpt: Staff will have more than one option for who receives these reports, including the RSO, and at least one executive who does not report to the RSO.
units.paraphrase: Staff have multiple report recipient options including the RSO and an independent executive.

units.excerpt: When we receive a report, we will promptly investigate, take appropriate and proportional corrective action if it is substantiated, and document the report and our findings.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will promptly investigate reports, take corrective action if substantiated, and document findings.

units.excerpt: We will provide quarterly updates to the Board regarding reports of potential noncompliance, whether substantiated or not.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will give the Board quarterly updates on noncompliance reports regardless of substantiation.

units.excerpt: If we determine that a report is (1) substantiated and (2) involves a material safety risk, we will promptly notify the Board and we may provide public notice of the same.
units.paraphrase: Substantiated reports involving material safety risk trigger prompt Board notification and possible public notice.

units.excerpt: Finally, we will protect reporters from retaliation, and where a report concerns the conduct of the RSO, at least one recipient will be a member of the Board.
units.paraphrase: Reporters are protected from retaliation, and RSO-related reports must go to at least one Board member.

units.excerpt: Employee agreements: We will not impose contractual non-disparagement obligations on employees, candidates, or former employees in a way that could impede or discourage them from publicly raising safety concerns about Anthropic.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will not impose non-disparagement clauses that could discourage raising safety concerns.

units.excerpt: If we offer agreements with a non-disparagement clause, that clause will not preclude raising safety concerns, nor will it preclude disclosure of the existence of that clause.
units.paraphrase: Any non-disparagement clause offered will not block raising safety concerns or disclosing the clause's existence.

units.excerpt: Internal review: We will regularly conduct an internal review of our implementation of this policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will regularly conduct internal reviews of policy implementation.

units.excerpt: Procedural compliance review: On approximately an annual basis, we will commission a third-party review that assesses whether we adhered to this policy's main procedural commitments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will commission an annual third-party review of procedural compliance with the policy.

units.excerpt: This review will focus on procedural compliance, not substantive outcomes.
units.paraphrase: The third-party review focuses on procedure, not substantive outcomes.

units.excerpt: Policy changes: Changes to the RSP will be proposed by the CEO and RSO, and approved by the Board in consultation with the LTBT.
units.paraphrase: RSP changes are proposed by the CEO and RSO and approved by the Board with LTBT consultation.

units.excerpt: If we update the RSP, we will publicly share the updated version prior to or on its effective date and will record the differences from the prior draft in the Change Log.
units.paraphrase: Updated RSP versions will be publicly shared by their effective date with differences recorded in the Change Log.

units.excerpt: We will maintain the current version of the RSP on our website.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will keep the current RSP version published on its website.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.excerpt: These commitments are necessarily high-level and limited. In many cases, we will not have enough information to determine that the relevant scenario applies and will have to use our best judgment to deal with uncertainty.
units.paraphrase: The competitor-related commitments are high-level and limited, requiring judgment amid uncertainty about scenario applicability.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.excerpt: But to the extent that other relevant AI developers prioritize safety and invest in legible demonstrations that they are doing so—as we intend to—commitments like this may help avoid an inadvertent "race to the bottom" on safety.
units.paraphrase: If other developers similarly prioritize and demonstrate safety, these commitments may help prevent a race to the bottom.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.excerpt: Further, the commitments below do not preclude us from taking cautionary action, such as refraining from training or deploying models, in other circumstances.
units.paraphrase: The listed commitments do not limit Anthropic from taking additional cautionary action in other situations.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.excerpt: Mitigating the risks from our models is a top priority for us, and we would strongly consider pausing development and/or deployment to improve the safety profiles of our models even in cases not covered below.
units.paraphrase: Risk mitigation is a top priority, and Anthropic would consider pausing development or deployment beyond the listed scenarios.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.locator: Table / Anthropic in the lead / Scenario
units.context_stem: Row: Anthropic in the lead. Column: Scenario.
units.excerpt: We have developed or will imminently develop a highly capable model; and we have clear evidence that no other competitor will soon develop such a model.
units.paraphrase: The scenario is Anthropic developing or nearly developing a highly capable model with no near-term competitor equivalent.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.locator: Table / Anthropic in the lead / Commitment
units.context_stem: Row: Anthropic in the lead. Column: Commitment.
units.excerpt: We will require a strong argument that catastrophic risk is contained, along the lines of our recommendations for industry-wide safety (see Section 1).
units.paraphrase: In this scenario Anthropic will require a strong argument that catastrophic risk is contained.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.locator: Table / Anthropic in the lead / Commitment
units.context_stem: Row: Anthropic in the lead. Column: Commitment.
units.excerpt: We will delay AI development and deployment as needed to achieve this, until and unless we no longer believe we have a significant lead.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will delay development and deployment as needed until it no longer believes it has a significant lead.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.locator: Table / Competitors have strong safety measures / Scenario
units.context_stem: Row: Competitors have strong safety measures. Column: Scenario.
units.excerpt: We have strong evidence that all competitors who have developed, or will soon develop, a highly capable frontier model are able to make strong arguments that catastrophic risk is contained, in the spirit of our recommendations for industry-wide safety (see Section 1).
units.paraphrase: The scenario is strong evidence that all relevant competitors can argue catastrophic risk is contained.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.locator: Table / Competitors have strong safety measures / Commitment
units.context_stem: Row: Competitors have strong safety measures. Column: Commitment.
units.excerpt: For our highly capable frontier models, we will meet or exceed the overall risk reduction posture of these competitors, as far as we can tell based on our best efforts to assess that posture.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will meet or exceed competitors' risk reduction posture for its highly capable models, as best it can assess.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.locator: Table / Competitors have strong safety measures / Commitment
units.context_stem: Row: Competitors have strong safety measures. Column: Commitment.
units.excerpt: Until we are able to do so, we will delay AI development and deployment as needed to achieve this.
units.paraphrase: Until able to meet or exceed that posture, Anthropic will delay development and deployment as needed.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.context_stem: Row: General upleveling. Column: Scenario. We have strong evidence that a competitor has implemented a risk mitigation that:
units.excerpt: (1) represents a significant improvement on reduction of our prioritized risks relative to our analogous mitigations; and
units.paraphrase: First condition: the competitor mitigation significantly improves on risk reduction relative to Anthropic's analogous mitigations.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.context_stem: Row: General upleveling. Column: Scenario. We have strong evidence that a competitor has implemented a risk mitigation that:
units.excerpt: (2) we could implement at comparable (or lower) effort or cost to our competitor.
units.paraphrase: Second condition: Anthropic could implement the mitigation at comparable or lower effort or cost.

units.section_heading: Appendix A: Commitments Related to Competitors
units.excerpt: We will make a significant effort to meet or exceed that performance standard. However, we will not necessarily delay AI development and deployment in this scenario.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will try to meet or exceed the competitor's mitigation standard but will not necessarily delay development or deployment.

units.excerpt: Earlier editions of our RSP defined "AI Safety Levels" with specific lists of required controls.
units.paraphrase: Prior RSP editions defined AI Safety Levels via specific control lists.

units.excerpt: We still use this concept to refer to, and distinguish between, present levels of risk mitigations—those that we maintain for existing AI models. (For example, our initial Risk Report uses this distinction.)
units.paraphrase: The ASL concept is still used to describe present mitigation levels for existing models, as in the initial Risk Report.

units.excerpt: However, when defining the risk mitigations needed for future levels of AI capability, we have found that providing a specific list of controls is overly rigid, and we instead prefer to focus on what sort of argument an AI developer should make (and what sorts of actors it should address) regarding the risk level from its systems.
units.paraphrase: For future capability levels, Anthropic prefers argument-based framing over rigid control lists.

units.excerpt: This and other italicized instances of "highly capable" use the term as defined in Section 3.6.
units.paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that italicized "highly capable" refers to the Section 3.6 definition.

units.excerpt: September 19, 2023 (RSP v1.0) RSP-2023 (aka RSP v1.0): Initial version.
units.paraphrase: The changelog notes RSP v1.0 was the initial version, dated September 19, 2023.

units.excerpt: RSP-2024: This update introduces a more flexible and nuanced approach to assessing and managing AI risks while maintaining our commitment not to train or deploy models unless we have implemented adequate safeguards.
units.paraphrase: The 2024 update adopts a more flexible risk approach while retaining the adequate-safeguards commitment.

units.excerpt: Key improvements include new capability thresholds to indicate when we should upgrade our safeguards, refined processes for evaluating model capabilities and the adequacy of our safeguards (inspired by safety case methodologies), and new measures for internal governance and external input.
units.paraphrase: Key 2024 improvements include new capability thresholds, refined evaluation processes, and new governance/external-input measures.

units.excerpt: We describe the most notable changes below.
units.paraphrase: The changelog will describe the most notable 2024 changes below.

units.excerpt: ASL definition changed: The term "ASL" now refers to groups of technical and operational safeguards (it previously also referred to models).
units.paraphrase: ASL now refers only to safeguard groups, not models as before.

units.excerpt: We also introduced the new concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards. This change allows for more targeted application of safeguards based on specific capabilities, rather than broad model categories.
units.paraphrase: New concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards allow targeted rather than broad-category safeguard application.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: ARA threshold now a checkpoint: We replaced our previous autonomous replication and adaption (ARA) threshold with a "checkpoint" for autonomous AI capabilities.
units.paraphrase: The ARA threshold was replaced with an autonomous-capability checkpoint.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: Rather than triggering higher safety standards automatically, reaching this checkpoint will prompt additional evaluation of the model's capabilities and accelerate our preparation of stronger safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Reaching the checkpoint prompts more evaluation and accelerated safeguard preparation rather than automatic escalation.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: We previously considered these capabilities as a trigger for increased safeguards, motivated by an attempt to establish some threshold while we developed a better sense of potential threats.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic previously treated these capabilities as a safeguard trigger to establish an initial threshold amid uncertainty.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
units.excerpt: We now believe that these capabilities - at the levels we initially considered - would not necessitate the ASL-3 standard.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic now believes these capability levels do not require the ASL-3 standard.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / AI R&D threshold added
units.excerpt: AI R&D threshold added: We added a new threshold for AI systems that can significantly advance AI development.
units.paraphrase: A new threshold was added for AI systems significantly advancing AI development.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / AI R&D threshold added
units.excerpt: Such capabilities could lead to rapid, unpredictable advances in AI, potentially outpacing our ability to evaluate and address emerging risks, and may also serve as an early warning sign for the ability to automate R&D in other domains.
units.paraphrase: These capabilities could enable rapid unpredictable AI advances and signal potential for automating R&D elsewhere.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: Testing for Capability Thresholds: Rather than using prespecified evaluations, we now require an affirmative case that models are sufficiently far from Capability Thresholds.
units.paraphrase: Testing now requires an affirmative case of distance from Capability Thresholds instead of prespecified evaluations.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: Predefined tests may miss emerging risks or be overly conservative relative to the actual threshold of concern.
units.paraphrase: Predefined tests risk missing emerging threats or being overly conservative.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
units.excerpt: Our most accurate tests change frequently enough that it is more practical to use this new approach than to have our Board pre-approve evaluations.
units.paraphrase: Since accurate tests change often, the new approach is more practical than Board pre-approval of evaluations.

units.excerpt: Adjusted evaluation cadence: We adjusted the comprehensive assessment cadence to 4x Effective Compute or six months of accumulated post-training enhancements (this was previously three months).
units.paraphrase: The comprehensive assessment cadence changed to 4x Effective Compute or six months of post-training enhancements, up from three months.

units.excerpt: We found that a three-month cadence forced teams to prioritize conducting frequent evaluations over more comprehensive testing and improving methodologies.
units.paraphrase: A three-month cadence had forced teams to prioritize frequency over comprehensive testing and methodology improvement.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
units.excerpt: Less prescriptive evaluation methodology: We have replaced some specifics in our previous testing methodology (e.g., using 1% of compute for elicitation or creating a 6x buffer), with more general requirements to (a) match expected efforts of potential adversaries and (b) provide informal estimates of how further scaling and research developments will impact model capabilities and performance on the same tasks.
units.paraphrase: Specific testing parameters like 1% compute elicitation and 6x buffer were replaced with general requirements to match adversary effort and estimate scaling impacts.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
units.excerpt: We have found that specific methodologies may become outdated when new research developments are introduced.
units.paraphrase: Specific methodologies risk becoming outdated as new research emerges.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
units.excerpt: Although still an aspirational goal, the science of evaluations is not currently mature enough to make confident predictions about the precise buffer we should require between current models and a Capability Threshold.
units.paraphrase: Evaluation science is not yet mature enough to precisely define the required buffer to a Capability Threshold, though this remains an aspiration.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
units.excerpt: More outcome-focused safeguard requirements: We have updated our ASL-3 safeguards requirements to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 safeguard requirements were updated to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
units.excerpt: Rather than detailing specific operational and technical safeguards, we now specify the overall security or deployment standards and requirements for meeting them.
units.paraphrase: Instead of specific safeguards, overall security or deployment standards and their requirements are now specified.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
units.excerpt: This is to allow us to adapt our safeguards more flexibly as our understanding of risks and possible safeguards improves.
units.paraphrase: The outcome-focused approach allows more flexible safeguard adaptation as understanding improves.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
units.excerpt: Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models: We have clarified which actors are in and out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard.
units.paraphrase: The 2024 update clarifies which actors are in or out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
units.excerpt: We also removed the commitment to protect against scaled attacks and distillation attacks from the ASL-2 Security standard.
units.paraphrase: The commitment to protect against scaled and distillation attacks was removed from the ASL-2 standard.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
units.excerpt: While distillation remains a concern for more capable models, models stored under ASL-2 safeguards have not yet reached potentially harmful Capability Thresholds.
units.paraphrase: Distillation is still a concern for more capable models, but ASL-2 models have not reached harmful thresholds.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
units.excerpt: Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users: We have updated the ASL-3 Deployment Standard to allow for different levels of safeguards based on deployment context.
units.paraphrase: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard now varies safeguard levels by deployment context.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
units.excerpt: For any general access systems, we still require passing intensive red-teaming.
units.paraphrase: General access systems still require passing intensive red-teaming.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
units.excerpt: For internal use, safety testing and deployments to sufficiently trusted users, we will instead require a combination of access controls and monitoring.
units.paraphrase: For internal use, safety testing, and trusted-user deployments, access controls and monitoring are required instead.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
units.excerpt: New Capability and Safeguards Reports: We have introduced Capability Reports and Safeguard Reports.
units.paraphrase: New Capability Reports and Safeguard Reports were introduced.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
units.excerpt: We expect that aggregating all the available evidence about model capabilities will provide decision makers with a more complete picture of the overall level of risk and improve our ability to solicit feedback on our work.
units.paraphrase: Aggregating capability evidence is expected to improve risk understanding and feedback solicitation.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Internal and external accountability
units.excerpt: Internal and external accountability: We have made a number of changes to our previous "procedural commitments."
units.paraphrase: Several changes were made to prior procedural commitments.

units.locator: Changelog / v2.0 / Internal and external accountability
units.excerpt: These include expanding the duties of the Responsible Scaling Officer; adding internal critique and external expert input on capability and safeguard assessments; new procedures related to internal governance; and maintaining a public page for overviews of past Capability and Safeguard Reports, RSP-related updates, and future plans.
units.paraphrase: Changes include expanded RSO duties, added internal/external input on assessments, new governance procedures, and a public reports/updates page.

units.excerpt: March 31, 2025 (RSP v2.1) RSP-2025: This update clarifies which Capability Thresholds would require enhanced safeguards beyond our current ASL-3 standards.
units.paraphrase: The v2.1 update clarifies which Capability Thresholds require safeguards beyond ASL-3.

units.excerpt: New Capability Thresholds: We have added a new capability threshold related to CBRN development, which defines capabilities that could substantially uplift the development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs.
units.paraphrase: A new CBRN-related capability threshold was added for capabilities that could uplift moderately resourced state programs.

units.excerpt: We have also disaggregated our existing AI R&D capability thresholds, separating them into two distinct levels (the ability to fully automate entry-level AI research work, and the ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling) and provided additional detail on the corresponding Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D thresholds were split into two levels—entry-level automation and dramatic scaling acceleration—with more detail on required safeguards.

units.excerpt: Iterative Commitment: We have adopted a general commitment to reevaluate our Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade to a new set of Required Safeguards.
units.paraphrase: A general commitment was adopted to reevaluate Capability Thresholds whenever Required Safeguards are upgraded.

units.excerpt: We have decided not to maintain a commitment to define ASL-N+1 evaluations by the time we develop ASL-N models; such an approach would add unnecessary complexity because Capability Thresholds do not naturally come grouped in discrete levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic dropped the commitment to predefine next-level evaluations, as thresholds do not group into discrete levels.

units.excerpt: We believe it is more practical and sensible instead to commit to reconsidering the whole list of Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade our safeguards.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic prefers reconsidering the full threshold list at each safeguard upgrade instead.

units.excerpt: May 14, 2025 (RSP v2.2) ASL-3 Security: This update excludes both sophisticated insiders and state-compromised insiders from the ASL-3 Security Standard.
units.paraphrase: The v2.2 update excludes sophisticated insiders and state-compromised insiders from the ASL-3 Security Standard.

units.excerpt: Previously, only "highly sophisticated state-compromised insiders" were explicitly excluded.
units.paraphrase: Previously only highly sophisticated state-compromised insiders were explicitly excluded.

units.excerpt: The model capabilities and threat models corresponding with the ASL-3 Security Standard do not warrant protection against either group: the CBRN-3 threat models entail large numbers of users having access to unguarded models (which is more likely to occur through a universal jailbreak than via model theft), and the relatively small number of employees who might be capable of model theft does not significantly affect the risk level.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 threat models do not warrant protection against these insider groups because CBRN-3 risk arises more from jailbreaks than theft, and few employees could achieve theft.

units.excerpt: For AI R&D-4, the threat models generally do not depend on model weight theft and instead entail AI systems engaging in autonomous internal sabotage.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D-4 threat models depend on autonomous internal sabotage rather than weight theft.

units.excerpt: February 24, 2026 (RSP v3.0) This update is a comprehensive rewrite of our RSP. For a summary of changes and the thinking behind them, see here.
units.paraphrase: The v3.0 update is described as a comprehensive rewrite, with a separate summary referenced.

units.excerpt: April 2, 2026 (RSP v3.1) This revision addresses the following points: (1) how we operationalize the Automated R&D capability threshold; (2) how we use internal feedback on Risk Reports; and (3) that we may consider pausing development or deployment even where the commitments described in Appendix A are not triggered.
units.paraphrase: The v3.1 revision covers operationalizing the Automated R&D threshold, use of internal Risk Report feedback, and possible pausing beyond Appendix A triggers.

units.excerpt: These changes are mostly clarificatory in nature; we don't see them as significant changes to substance.
units.paraphrase: The v3.1 changes are mostly clarificatory rather than substantive.

units.excerpt: Change (1) reflects further discussion of our operationalization of the capability threshold, and involves some substantive changes to make it better reflect our underlying intent.
units.paraphrase: The Automated R&D threshold change involves some substantive revision to better reflect intent.

units.excerpt: This update also includes minor edits for style or clarity.
units.paraphrase: The v3.1 update also includes minor style or clarity edits.

units.excerpt: April 29, 2026 (RSP v3.2) This update authorizes the LTBT to request external review of Risk Reports, gives the LTBT the power to approve our selection of external reviewers, and formalizes a requirement that we provide the LTBT with regular briefings.
units.paraphrase: The v3.2 update gives the LTBT power to request external review, approve reviewer selection, and formalizes regular LTBT briefings.

units.excerpt: May 26, 2026 (RSP v3.3) This update (1) revises our threshold for novel chemical/biological weapons production to better track the threat model of concern; (2) refines our approach to off-cycle updates regarding the risks of individual models; and (3) makes minor terminology changes.
units.paraphrase: The current v3.3 update revises the CBRN production threshold, refines off-cycle model risk update processes, and makes minor terminology changes.

excerpt: It adjusts the scope of Risk Reports to cover Anthropic's models and activities as of a given coverage date up to 30 days prior to that report's publication.
paraphrase: Change 3 adjusts Risk Report scope to cover a coverage date up to 30 days before publication.

context_stem: This update makes five changes: (3) coverage date adjustment.
excerpt: We aim to hold our Risk Reports to a higher standard of thoroughness and coverage than our system cards while operating on a longer cadence and staying applicable over several months, and expect this change to make it easier to meet this standard without having to incorporate very recent updates to Anthropic's activities on short notice.
paraphrase: Anthropic aims for Risk Reports to be more thorough than system cards while covering longer periods, and expects this change to ease meeting that standard without last-minute updates.

excerpt: It requires us to publicly disclose, at a high level, when we make redactions in the public version of a Risk Report. Our previous Risk Report already meets this standard.
paraphrase: Change 4 requires high-level public disclosure of redactions in Risk Reports; the previous report already meets this standard.

excerpt: It clarifies that external review of our Risk Reports can involve multiple external reviewers reviewing different unredacted sections of the Risk Report, so long as all parts of the unredacted report are evaluated by at least one external reviewer.
paraphrase: Change 5 clarifies that multiple external reviewers may each review different unredacted sections, provided every part is reviewed by at least one reviewer.

excerpt: It also contains minor typo and formatting corrections.
paraphrase: The update also includes minor typo and formatting corrections.
